interviewQuestions.question: Replication lag just spiked — what breaks, and how do you defend against it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with the concrete symptom rather than the abstract fact that replicas lag: a user posts something, refreshes, and it's gone because their read landed on a replica that hasn't caught up yet — or two users see contradictory versions of the same object.

For defense, I'd combine a few things. Read-after-write routing sends a user's own subsequent reads to the primary (or a replica confirmed caught up) for a short window after they write. Lag monitoring emits each replica's lag as a metric and alerts when it crosses a threshold — say 2 seconds — well before users notice. Health checks pull a badly lagging replica out of the read pool entirely.

I'd also chase the root cause: if a bulk job is what's spiking lag, throttling or rescheduling that job fixes the actual cause instead of just routing around the symptom.

**Testing:** whether you can name a concrete failure and a concrete mitigation, not just repeat that replicas can lag.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Defending against a replication lag spike

interviewQuestions.question: How would you detect that replication lag has grown before users start complaining?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't wait for a support ticket — every replica can report how far behind the primary it is, typically as a log-position or WAL-offset gap that converts cleanly into an estimated time lag. I'd emit that as a per-replica metric and graph it continuously.

On top of the graph, I'd set an alert threshold meaningfully below the point where users would actually notice — for example, alert at 2 seconds if the read-after-write window is a few seconds, giving the team time to react before it becomes user-visible.

I'd also tie the alert to context: which replica, and whether a known write-heavy job is running at the same time, so the on-call engineer isn't starting from zero when it fires.

**Testing:** whether you design for detection proactively, rather than treating user complaints as the monitoring system.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Detecting lag before it's a complaint

interviewQuestions.question: The bulk write job is the actual root cause of the lag spike — do you fix the symptom or the root cause?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Both, on different timelines. Short-term, I'd apply read-after-write routing or a replica health check so users stop seeing the symptom right now — that's a mitigation, not a fix, and I'd say so explicitly rather than pretending it solves the underlying problem.

Longer-term, I'd address the actual cause: throttle the bulk job's write rate, reschedule it to a low-traffic window, or run it against a dedicated replica that read traffic never touches, so it can't saturate the replication stream that live reads depend on.

I'd frame it to the interviewer as sequencing, not a choice between the two — stop the user-visible pain immediately, then remove the recurring cause so the same incident doesn't happen again next time that job runs.

**Testing:** whether you can separate an immediate mitigation from a durable fix, and commit to doing both.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Symptom fix vs root-cause fix
